{{Gymnastics at the 2020 Summer Olympics}}

The women's [[floor (gymnastics)|floor]] event at the [[2020 Summer Olympics]] was held on 25 July and 2 August 2021 at the [[Ariake Gymnastics Centre]].<ref name=dates>{{cite web|url=https://tokyo2020.org/en/schedule/artistic-gymnastics-schedule |title=Artistic Gymnastics Competition Schedule |publisher=Tokyo 2020 |accessdate=30 November 2020 }}</ref> Approximately 85 gymnasts from 53 nations (of the 98 total gymnasts) competed on floor in the qualifying round.<ref name=qualifying>{{cite web |url = https://www.gymnastics.sport/publicdir/rules/files/en_Olympic%20Qualification%20System%20Tokyo%202020%20ART.pdf |title = Qualification System – Games of the XXXII Olympiad – ''Artistic Gymnastics'' |publisher = [[International Gymnastics Federation]] |format = [[PDF]] |accessdate = 30 November 2020}}</ref>

[[Jade Carey]] won the competition, earning the [[United States at the 2020 Summer Olympics|United States]]' third consecutive title on floor. The title is Carey's first Olympic medal. [[Italy at the 2020 Summer Olympics|Italy]]'s [[Vanessa Ferrari]] earned silver to win her first Olympic medal, as well Italy's first individual Olympic medal in women's artistic gymnastics and second-ever medal overall. [[Mai Murakami]] of [[Japan at the 2020 Summer Olympics|Japan]] and [[Angelina Melnikova]] of [[Russian Olympic Committee athletes at the 2020 Summer Olympics|ROC]] tied for the bronze. It is Murakami's first Olympic medal and Melnikova's fourth. Like Ferrari, Murakami's medal is also the first individual Olympic medal for her country in women's artistic gymnastics and second-ever overall.
{{TOC limit|3}}

The medals for the competition were presented by [[Octavian Morariu]], [[Romania]]; [[List of members of the International Olympic Committee|IOC Member]], and the medalists' bouquets were presented by [[Farid Gayibov]], [[Azerbaijan]]; [[International Gymnastics Federation|FIG Executive Committee Member]].

== Background ==
This was the 19th appearance of the event, after making its debut at the [[1952 Summer Olympics]]. Defending champion [[Simone Biles]] of the [[United States at the 2020 Summer Olympics|United States]] was aiming to become the first woman to defend their title since [[Nellie Kim]] in 1976 and 1980. Representing Italy, [[Vanessa Ferrari]] has returned for her fourth [[Olympic Games]], hoping to leave with a medal after coming shy of bronze in 2012 and 2016.<ref>{{Cite web |last=DeMeyer • • |first=Tess |title=Italian Gymnast Vanessa Ferrari Wins First Olympic Medal at 30 Years Old |url=https://www.nbcdfw.com/news/sports/tokyo-summer-olympics/italian-gymnast-vanessa-ferrari-wins-first-olympic-medal-at-30-years-old/2703756/ |access-date=2022-05-09 |website=NBC 5 Dallas-Fort Worth |language=en-US}}</ref> Biles qualified in second place behind Ferrari after a relatively subpar performance by her standards.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2021/07/25/sports/olympics/simone-biles-floor-exercise.html|title=Simone Biles starts Olympics with a floor exercise that isn’t up to her usual standards.|first=Juliet|last=Macur|website=[[The New York Times]]|date=25 July 2021}}</ref> However, she announced her withdrawal on 31 July 2021 due to continued mental blocks, following earlier withdrawals from the team and individual all-around finals, as well as the first day of individual event finals.<ref name=biles>{{cite web|url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/sports/olympics/2021/07/31/simone-biles-withdraws-floor-exercise-final-tokyo-olympics/5445648001/|title=Simone Biles withdraws from floor exercise final at Olympics; status for balance beam unclear|first=Nancy|last=Armour|website=[[USA Today]]|date=31 July 2021}}</ref>

== Qualification ==
{{main|Gymnastics at the 2020 Summer Olympics – Qualification}}

A [[National Olympic Committee]] (NOC) could enter up to 6 qualified gymnasts: a team of 4 and up to 2 specialists. A total of 98 quota places are allocated to women's gymnastics.

The 12 teams that qualify will be able to send 4 gymnasts in the team competition, for a total of 48 of the 98 quota places. The top three teams at the [[2018 World Artistic Gymnastics Championships]] (the United States, Russia, and China) and the top nine teams (excluding those already qualified) at the [[2019 World Artistic Gymnastics Championships]] (France, Canada, the Netherlands, Great Britain, Italy, Germany, Belgium, Japan, and Spain) earned team qualification places. The US Women's Gymnastics Olympic Team consisted of returner Simone Biles, Jordan Chiles, Sunisa Lee and Grace McCullum; with individuals MyKayla Skinner and Jade Carey.<ref>{{Cite web |title=USA Gymnastics {{!}} 2020 Olympic Games Results |url=https://usagym.org/pages/events/2021/olympicsresults.html |access-date=2022-05-09 |website=usagym.org}}</ref>

The remaining 50 quota places are awarded individually. Each gymnast can only earn one place, except that gymnasts that competed with a team that qualified are eligible to earn a second place through the 2020 All Around World Cup Series. Some of the individual events are open to gymnasts from NOCs with qualified teams, while others are not. These places are filled through various criteria based on the 2019 World Championships, the [[2020 FIG Artistic Gymnastics World Cup series]], continental championships, a host guarantee, and a Tripartite Commission invitation. 

Each of the 98 qualified gymnasts are eligible for the floor competition, but many gymnasts do not compete in each of the apparatus events.

The [[COVID-19 pandemic]] delayed many of the events for qualifying for gymnastics. The 2018 and 2019 World Championships were completed on time, but many of the World Cup series events were delayed into 2021.

== Competition format ==
The top 8 qualifiers in the [[Gymnastics at the 2020 Summer Olympics – Women's artistic qualification|qualification phase]] (limit two per NOC) advanced to the apparatus final. The finalists performed on the floor again. Qualification scores were then ignored, with only final round scores counting.

== Schedule ==
The competition was held over two days, 25 July and 2 August. The qualifying round (for all women's gymnastics events) was the first day with the floor final on the third and final day of individual event finals.<ref name=dates/>

The reserves for the women's floor final were:
# {{flagIOCathlete|[[Jennifer Gadirova]]|GBR|2020 Summer}} – ''called up after [[Simone Biles]]' withdrawal'' <ref name=biles/>
# {{flagIOCathlete|[[Nina Derwael]]|BEL|2020 Summer}}

Only two gymnasts from each country may advance to the event final. No gymnasts were excluded from the final because of the quota, although ROC gymnasts [[Vladislava Urazova]] and [[Lilia Akhaimova]], and American gymnasts [[Jordan Chiles]] and [[MyKayla Skinner]] were excluded as reserves due to the two-per-country rule.

Bronze medalists [[Mai Murakami]] and [[Angelina Melnikova]] had identical E-scores (8.266), and also identical D-scores (5.9), meaning that the tie was unbroken per FIG's standard tie-breaking procedures.<ref name="FIG01a">{{cite web|url=https://www.gymnastics.sport/publicdir/rules/files/en_Technical%20Regulations%202021%20changes.pdf|title=Technical Regulations 2020 (amended, valid until 31.12.2021)|publisher=[[International Gymnastics Federation]]|accessdate=1 August 2021|quote=Apparatus Finals<br>In case of a tie, in points of the final score at any place on all apparatus except for vault, the ranking will be determined by the following criteria:<br>1. the gymnast with the highest E-score prevails<br>2. the gymnast with the highest D-score prevails<br>If they remain tied, the gymnasts will share the same classification}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://olympics.com/tokyo-2020/olympic-games/resOG2020-/pdf/OG2020-/GAR/OG2020-_GAR_C77A_GARW1APFX-------------FNL---------.pdf|title=Artistic Gymnastics: Women's Floor Exercise Final – Tie Break Report|publisher=[[International Olympic Committee]]|access-date=2 August 2021|archive-date=2 August 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210802100332/https://olympics.com/tokyo-2020/olympic-games/resOG2020-/pdf/OG2020-/GAR/OG2020-_GAR_C77A_GARW1APFX-------------FNL---------.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://olympics.com/tokyo-2020/olympic-games/resOG2020-/pdf/OG2020-/GAR/OG2020-_GAR_C73I_GARW1APFX-------------FNL---------.pdf|title=Artistic Gymnastics: Women's Floor Exercise Final – Results|publisher=[[International Olympic Committee]]|access-date=2 August 2021|archive-date=2 August 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210802094448/https://olympics.com/tokyo-2020/olympic-games/resOG2020-/pdf/OG2020-/GAR/OG2020-_GAR_C73I_GARW1APFX-------------FNL---------.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref> Practically, this also means that both gymnasts would be awarded the same rank, which is very rare today, and this is the first time since 1996 to have a tie on the podium in men's and women's [[artistic gymnastics]] when current Olympic-tie-breaking rules took effect at the [[2000 Summer Olympics|2000 Sydney Games]].

[[Jade Carey]] earned the US's third consecutive gold medal in the floor event for the past three Olympics.<ref>{{Cite web |title=2020 Tokyo Olympics: Jade Carey wins gold in women's floor exercise for Team USA |url=https://www.cbssports.com/olympics/news/2020-tokyo-olympics-jade-carey-wins-gold-in-womens-floor-exercise-for-team-usa/ |access-date=2022-05-09 |website=CBSSports.com |language=en}}</ref> [[Vanessa Ferrari]] at the age of 30 finally got her Olympic medal on floor, after placing 4th at the 2012 and 2016 Olympics. She scored third highest in the floor final at the [[Gymnastics at the 2012 Summer Olympics – Women's floor|2012 London Olympics]], but the tie-breaking procedure worked against her to rank her fourth and out of the medals in the standings.
